deleted.text: An event happens at one well-defined instant, the same for every attendee.
Every event start is stored as a UTC instant in the anchor column, and this value is called the anchor instant.
A recurring series is the anchor instant plus a repeat interval counted in whole hours, so a weekly series repeats every 168 hours.
The organizer's zone is kept only as a display hint and plays no part in scheduling.
anchor_utc
timestamp
Start of the first occurrence as a UTC instant
interval_hours
integer
Hours between two occurrences, empty for a single event
display_zone
text
Zone shown to the organizer, unused by scheduling
The expander reads a series and adds the repeat interval to the anchor instant until it leaves the requested window.
Each result is already a UTC instant, so expansion needs no zone data and runs as plain integer arithmetic.
Exceptions such as a moved or cancelled occurrence are stored as overrides keyed by the occurrence's original instant.
An override replaces the computed occurrence when the expander reaches that instant.
Because the interval is fixed in hours, a weekly 09:00 meeting in Berlin moves to 08:00 local time after the autumn change and back to 09:00 after the spring change.
Attendees in zones without daylight saving see no shift at all.
Twice a year the rebase job finds recurring series whose display zone changed its offset and emails their organizers, asking them to re-save the series at the intended local hour.
Re-saving writes a new anchor instant from the next occurrence onward and keeps earlier occurrences unchanged.
A reminder is an offset before an occurrence, such as 15 minutes or one day.
The reminder worker expands each series for the next 48 hours every five minutes and enqueues one job per reminder at the occurrence's instant minus the offset.
After a transition, reminders follow the anchor instant, so they fire at the shifted local hour until the organizer re-saves the series.
Each job carries the occurrence's instant so that a duplicate job for the same occurrence is dropped.
The API returns each occurrence with its UTC instant.
Clients render the time in the viewer's zone, which the web client reads from the browser and the user may override in settings.
The organizer view also shows the time in the display zone, so an organizer can notice when a series has drifted from its intended local hour.
The zone rules come from the IANA tz database, which publishes several releases a year as governments change their rules.
The operating system zone files on a host can lag behind those releases by months.
The service ships its own pinned copy of the tz database, used for display and by the rebase job.
A new release is adopted through an ordinary deployment.
It changes how times are displayed but never moves a stored occurrence.
Create and update requests carry the start as a UTC timestamp with a trailing Z, plus an optional display zone.
Imports from iCalendar files are accepted, and each local time in the file is converted to a UTC instant once, at import.
The test suite runs the expander against series in Europe/Berlin, America/Sao_Paulo, Australia/Lord_Howe and Asia/Kolkata.
Each case checks that occurrences stay exactly one interval apart across at least one spring and one autumn transition, and that the rebase job selects the series it should.
Whether the rebase job should re-save series automatically instead of emailing organizers.

candidates.sentence: The zone comes from the organizer's choice in the event form rather than from a guess based on the network address of the request.
The gap between two occurrences is not a fixed count of hours, since a week that crosses a transition is an hour shorter or longer.
This service does not materialise occurrences ahead of time, so an edit to a series touches a single row.
When a local time occurs twice in an autumn overlap, the expander takes the earlier of the two instants.
Organizers do not have to edit a series after a clock change to keep it at its usual hour.
There is no rebase job, and organizers receive no email around the spring and autumn clock changes.
Reminder jobs are written to the shared job queue rather than registered as cron entries on the worker hosts.
A reminder is never sent for an occurrence that has been cancelled or deleted.
When an event has no reminder setting, no notification is sent before it starts.
The service therefore does not read zone rules from the host but ships its own pinned copy of the tz database.
Create and update requests carry the start as a local date-time string without an offset, plus a zone field holding an IANA name.
The iCalendar standard allows a floating time that carries no zone at all.
The import endpoint does not accept floating times and asks the user to pick a zone instead.
Whether organizers should be able to change the zone of an existing series without moving its occurrences in local time.
